utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Court Deputy, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we are going to hear the witness, there is a matter that this Trial Chamber would like to mention. That is the Trial Chamber has been informed of the concerns expressed by Mr. Blagojevic regarding the decision of the Trial Chamber not to call Mr. Erdemovic for cross-examination. In order to ensure that no misunderstanding is made on what granted this decision, the Trial Chamber wishes to clarify a few points. First, the decision has already been rendered by this Trial Chamber and it is not subject to reconsideration. Like in all other decisions rendered by this Trial Chamber, it may not please both parties or one or the other party. The decision was made by the Trial Chamber in full independence while the arguments of both parties were heard and considered before the decision was reached. This decision is the decision of the Trial Chamber which does not reflect the position of the parties, but the position of the Trial Chamber. If, being aware of the decision process, Mr. Blagojevic still wants to examine Mr. Erdemovic as a witness, he still has the possibility to call him as a Defence witness in the future in his case. This is the explanation we would like to make concerning our decisions of not calling Mr. Erdemovic to be cross-examined. Yes, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much for considering so diligently these key issues. I must say that your work is of great assistance to me because I am alone in all these goings on. But I wish to point out one thing. At the end of the day, what we see here is an effort to push the view of the Prosecutor through the 92 bis statements and to shape opinions through these statements. It's a very dangerous situation, because the situation is shaped through 92 bis statements. I would like no shadow to overcast the truth that we are supposed to arrive at in considering a matter so important as Srebrenica. We should try to put an end to this and prevent the Prosecutor in these efforts, because matters are much more complicated than that. Because this international Tribunal should bring to justice those who are really responsible for what happened. Furthermore, Your Honours, allow me just to avail myself this opportunity to say one more thing in order not to take the floor again. In principle, I'm not happy with the cross-examination conducted, specifically with regard to witness Deronjic. But it seems that I am impotent to do anything about it. It all seems to me as a stage managed effort by the Defence that has been imposed on me, but there's nothing I can do about that either. I wish only to remind you of the 17th of December last year when the Prosecutor referred to three 92 bis witness, namely Erdemovic, Deronjic, and I believe Mrs. Rasim Begovic. If I understood correctly from subsequent information, because I was not informed at the time and I am learning as we speak the English language out of necessity, the Prosecutor spoke of the high degree of understanding between him and Mr. Karnavas. That's what I noted. This high degree of understanding seems to be to my detriment, I must say. Let's take, for instance, what my imposed Defence counsel said on the 19th of January when he said that they reached an agreement over Erdemovic. What that says to me is the following, and I deeply believe this: That the aforementioned person from my Defence team has joined the Prosecutor's team and is working against me. This is indefensible. I only wish to corroborate this with one substantive fact, and that is something that is in the transcript of the Milosevic trial of the 26th November, last year. It was not only Mr. Deronjic who was supposed to be heard here, but also Mr. Erdemovic, not for purposes of my defence, not because I wanted to accept or introduce the 92 bis statement of Erdemovic here. The Prosecutor wanted that. It was stage managed and its contents is not the truth, especially not the truth that goes in my favour. The same is true of the third witness. God only knows what will transpire in the future with regard to these witnesses. As I understand Your Honours, you ordered in the month of December that my illegal Defence submit a report on the status of my Defence case. We are now in the month of January and we still haven't got that report. I would like to know where I stand. In addition, two or three days ago a witness V80 was mentioned as another 92 bis witness. I have no idea who this witness is and what is being done with relation to him. I am supposed to rot in prison here for something that I am maybe not even guilty of. The indictment is being strengthened by the fact that my Defence is working against me. Please, I am begging for your understanding. I am only asking for what is fundamental and elementary to my rights. If we go on this way, this is the twilight of justice, not only the twilight of Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Mr. Blagojevic, for your statement. I think there are still some misunderstandings between us. As for the 92 bis witnesses, in the Rules and in the practice of this Tribunal, there are very strict Rules concerning of the admission of the evidence through 92 bis. And at the same time the Defence team will have the same right to introduce any evidence through 92 bis in their case in the future. There's no problem about that. Secondly, Mr. Blagojevic, I think you made a very serious allegation against your counsel. So far as I know you have to present some concrete evidence to verify your allegations. During the process of the proceedings in this Tribunal, the parties are encouraged by this Bench to meet each other to exchange views on such matters. If there's agreement between the parties mostly on the procedural matters, that will grateful facilitate the proceedings of this trial. As the a guarantor of the rights of the accused, this Trial Chamber will watch very carefully and review any result of the agreement the party has already reached. Up to now, we don't see any irregularities in this practice in this case. I think you misunderstand the meanings of our decisions in last December. We do not request Defence counsel to present his case to us. This is entirely his business. We just want the Defence counsel to file us a report on his relationship with you, Mr. Blagojevic, to see if there's any improvement between your relationship. We have no right to interfere into the communications between you and your counsel, Mr. Karnavas. As for the specific issue concerning of Mr. Deronjic's cross-examination, in our decisions rendered on the 15th January, 2004, we admitted the transcript as well as the previous statement by Mr. Deronjic into the evidence under 92 bis. And we only gave the limited direct examination to the Prosecution, that is certain matters regarding his reference to Mr. Blagojevic, while at the same time we gave the full right to the Defence counsel to cross-examine Mr. Deronjic in relation to all the evidence admitted. Of course we do not expect that cross-examination will take so long, but I could say many, many aspects, if I may say it more clearly, many, many more important aspects in the transcript or in his previous statement has been touched upon by Mr. Karnavas during the last two days. I hope that Mr. Karnavas could finish his cross-examination today because there are many witnesses waiting to testify, and some of them have been here in The Hague for a week. As I said before that the counsels and the Registrar is willing to help you to help yourself. She or he could explain to you the legal aspects of all the matters I mentioned today in very detail. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask him or her and try to get direct contact with your counsel, Mr. Karnavas, as soon as possible, because I understand that the Prosecution's case is approaching an end and the Defence case will start very soon. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During the Milosevic trial where you testified on 26th November, 2003, and I quote from page 29.702, you stated to Mr. Milosevic: "If you think that these killings were also part of my responsibility, I reacted to them as a human being. I had nothing to do -- it had nothing to do with my duties, with my official responsibilities." When you made that statement under oath a few months ago, was that a truthful statement as far as you understand it to be? I was quoting from lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, from lines 24, counsel, on page 29.702, going on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for background. Are we referring to Srebrenica and not Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall making that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that statement, but I cannot remember the entire contexts, although you did remind me a little by this quotation. I suppose the discussion was about Srebrenica. In response to which question was that answer made? You mentioned me reacting as a human being. I suppose it had something to do with the arrival of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did, and I think overall your responsibility. You go on to say: "I want to remind you that the complete staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska was present there, everyone from the Main Staff to brigade staff, all the relevant steps in the hierarchy were represented, including the police force. And with all that in mind, do you really think it was my job to secure those prisoners?" Do you recall making that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now I remember all of it. And of course I stand by my assertion that it was not my duty to provide security for those people. I was not given any such order, nor did I have anything to do with the prisoners and the security provided to them, meaning physical security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those prisoners, however, as we already discussed, were from the civilian population from Potocari or originating from Srebrenica, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Srebrenica, generally speaking. But you seem to omit the fact, or maybe you're not aware of it, that a great number of those prisoners were not brought from Potocari; a great number of them were taken prisoner in war operations in Konjevic Polje in combat. They were brought by the army, it was logical for the army to take care of their prisoners and to provide security. If you're talking about those who were singled out, a group of civilians who were brought from other places and placed in Potocari, I told you what the order of the president was, and I conveyed that order. I did continue to display interest in them and found out where they were detained. I found out that this group that was singled out was held in municipal city prisons and in the command of the brigade, in its prison quarters. I thought that this was sufficient, to say that they were adequately protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Leaving aside the prisoners of war, that is those who had been captured by the VRS forces or the special police as they were trying to make their way through the woods on to the safe territory, aside from those, are you suggesting that those boys and men from ages 16 or 15 all the way to 60 were not part of your official responsibilities, keeping in mind that you had a decision appointing you commissioner of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think that what you are saying, at least I wish to believe that you are saying it sincerely and without pathos. I had no information that a single boy from that group of civilians was singled out. I'm not saying that this never happened. On the contrary, I later heard that among the great group of people who were later killed, there were even boys and old men. However, I had no such information then. I told you that the information I had on the 12th was that some people were being singled out, and I said as much to the Prosecution, that people were being singled out, that a part of those prisoners who were separated from the others were in the military station in town and in the military prisons. I mentioned even the names of some of those people, but nobody told me that there were boys among them. You are saying that to me for the first time. I'm not saying that this didn't happen; I'm saying that I didn't know. Is it a fact that even those prisoners in the presence of General Mladic, the supreme commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, were singled out, separated from the others. The military police took part in that and logical to expect of them to take care of such prisoners, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you were given a mandate to protect those people in Potocari. Correct? Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please read where it is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm reading from the decision that was given to you. It's marked for identification purposes as P687. And it states that: "The commissioner shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and to assure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." And then if you go to paragraph 5 it says: "Decisions by the civilian commissioner shall," not may, but shall, "be binding for all civilian authority organs," that would include MUP, that would include the civilian police, in particular Mr. Borovcanin who you were instrumental in bringing over there. So given this mandate, sir, is it not a fact that one of your responsibilities was the well being of those who were being separated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I just told you to what people it referred and what I undertook. Do you have information that anybody in Bratunac was separated from general groups of prisoners taken out of prisons, executed, killed? They are all I know about. I don't know what happened to the others. You are insinuating very serious things and you are trying to misrepresent things to the Court. And you are even saying at some point that I was issuing orders to the brigade. If you are trying to make that out to be my responsibility, then we have to go back to the issue of my powers. Do you mean my de jure authorisations and powers to command? You are really not allowing me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you've had these explanations and we've heard them before. I'm trying to get a concrete answer from you. You had a responsibility to protect those civilians, including the men that were separated.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That is your understanding of your mandate under this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, have you established and proved that I had this decision at the time when we discussed that matter and when those things were going on? Have you reached that conclusion or are you insinuating that as well? I did not have such proof, and if you are claiming that I did, then you should state that and then we will discuss it. Secondly, that decision does not state what you are saying, neither can it be interpreted in that way. There is a sentence stating about the treatment of the prisoners of war. I asked the president from the command about the treatment of the prisoners of war. What do you imply under treatment? Yes, I apologise. I asked him: What do you imply by this treatment, Mr. President, because I don't have that paper with me. I told him ironically, Do you think I can command Mladic and ensure the proper treatment and the protection of those people, the prisoners of war. He said, Of course, Miroslav, I don't think you have that power. He laughed. He said, I know what your relations are with Mr. Mladic. He said I will convey orders to him about that. This is of course a clear thing. He is the supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Please wait, I have to finish. You are not allowing me -- well, first I have to say that it is very impolite --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will continue on Monday --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, please. What are you talking about? Monday, I have to finish my sentence. So the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... We will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the witness has given us a very important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has given us this information over and over again. He's trying to minimise his responsibility. I'm asking him a concrete question. He answered it. He said that he did not have the powers. I accept that if that's what his answer is. Now I'm ready to move on. We've heard his explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I wanted to say that this conversation with President Karadzic clarified for me my role regarding the treatment of the prisoners of war. He conveyed that to me and he said, and this is what I said in my statement, that I have to convey at an official meeting how the Serbian side -- we on the Serbian side should treat eventual prisoners of war which would be found amongst the civilians possibly. This is what the president meant when he was explaining my role to me in regard to this issue of the treatment, and I stated this at the Fontana publicly, even though Mladic did not want to state this openly, but I was convincing him to state it openly. I told him that the president told me that we do have the -- we are obliged under the conventions of war to act in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During that conversation, assuming that it took place over the phone, as you claim it to be, at no time did President Karadzic remind you or insinuate in any way about your alleged conversation that you had with him with respect to the Western Slavonia principle?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What telephone conversation? The Western Slavonia principle --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated that you managed to get all of this information from the telephone on the 11th. In the past, you have given conflicting interviews, one stating that you actually went to Pale on the 11th and had a personal meeting with President Karadzic. Here you seem to be denying that, saying that you didn't go on the 11th but rather you got all of your instructions on the telephone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Karnavas. You are making assertions and asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is what you -- this is your assertion today and yesterday and the day before, that you never went to Pale on the 11th, which would give you, obviously, the reason to come here today and say, I didn't have this decision physically in my hand. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you know that I had the interview on the 25th of November, 1993. That's what it states here. That's when I decided to say everything correctly when I gave the exact chronology and stated the exact facts. You are constantly dealing with the things that I said from the beginning were not true. For four days you are trying to establish that it is not true, what I had already said was not true. Please stick to this. All of this is absolutely correct, so that is what is correct. And I myself said that the previous things were not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So when you were giving false information to the Prosecutor, pushing it on to them as truthful, you wanted to be believed by them so you wouldn't be indicted. Now that you're indicted, somehow what you're saying all of a sudden must be the truth once again. Correct? So I guess the question is: The truth depends on what's good for Deronjic, if he's going to gain, if it's good for him, as in this case trying to get a nice comfortable deal from the Prosecution, then what you're saying must be the truth. So it all depends how you look at it. Isn't that a fact, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, just see how many allegations you've made in one question. If you're looking for a yes or no answer, I cannot give you such an answer. Allow me to deal with each one of your assertions, which are quite substantial, so I can give an explanation. I can see what this is all about. You are guessing about my motives even, why I told the truth now. And you determined that my motive is my benefit -- is self interest. But you could ask me if something is true or not. Instead of that, you are just making guesses and not asking me. Some things you are not even talking about. When I made my decision to admit my guilt, at the same time I made another decision. There are lawyers, they have their names, you can call them here to testify, and I suggest you call all three of them to testify. It's a shame that you didn't ask them to do so the day before when my lawyer was still here. I made the decision to testify. I have reasons, very important reasons, why I would want to do that. But I do not have to tell you about those reasons. But if the Trial Chamber asks me, I ask respond to that. My decision does not depend in the least on the offer from the Prosecution to make a deal. Let's leave Glogova aside. There was a statement about all the events that I participated in from the beginning of the war right until the end when I withdrew from politics. I will skip over Glogova only because I don't believe that we would agree on that question. I said, Tell the Prosecution I will testify about all of this regardless of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, I think the Defence counsel asked you a simple question, why previously you gave the incorrect statement until the last time. Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that my earlier statements were incorrect because there are several reasons, one of them I did mention, that was fear for my own safety or maybe my wrong thinking about wrong political implications if this truth were to come out, and ultimately I wanted to use my right which is well-known, that I am not obliged to tell the truth if it can harm me in any way at that point. So I did not give an entirely truthful statement for those reasons. But I do not agree that those statements are completely untrue. They are partially untrue, but Mr. Karnavas is making insinuations about that. And I cannot enter into a dispute about that with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, when you had this conversation with President Karadzic on the 11th of July from the command post of the Bratunac Brigade, that would have been two or three perhaps even four days after you had this conversation with President Karadzic in Pale where the Western Slavonia principle had been raised. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear -- I'm sorry, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll break it down. According to your testimony, once you decided to make an agreement, you claim that when you met with President Karadzic on the 8th or 9th or 10th, we're unclear of the date, that -- and you asked him what the intentions were for Srebrenica and you asked that Borovcanin be brought into the picture because you knew him and you wanted, I believe the word was, serious forces. At that point you claim that President Karadzic raised the issue of the Western Slavonia principle with respect to what should be done to the folks from Srebrenica in the eventuality Srebrenica were to fall. Do you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the question? Correct. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, and yesterday we established that we have no concrete evidence, physical evidence, either in written form or maybe an eyewitness who overheard the conversation and gave a statement, we have nothing other than, we have nothing other than, your testimony that this is what President Karadzic told you on that particular day. I'm talking about the conversation, not whether you were seen meeting with President Karadzic. I'm saying whether they heard it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were able to hear. They were close, but perhaps they were able to hear. But I don't think so. I cannot say one or the other. When you say I don't have any proof about this conversation, yes, I can agree with you there, there is no proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the 11th you get notice to go to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to telephone President Karadzic because you have learned that you have this new appointment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you indicate and your testimony, your firm testimony here in court, is that all of your instructions were received over the phone and perhaps later on, a few days later, this is your testimony now, you received -- you physically received the copy of the decision. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less that's correct. I would not say all the explanations, because we cannot predict any situation -- every situation that would happen, but in essence, yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was during this conversation where you had expressed with some degree of assertiveness to President Karadzic that you would have a difficult time carrying out part of your task, at least as it related to General Mladic, because there had been, you know, some history between the two of you, and in fact Mladic didn't get along with Karadzic either. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I suppose that that conversation, because it was taking place in a secure environment, which is why you went to the Bratunac Brigade, took some time, a few moments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And during this conversation, at no time -- at least we don't see it in any of your statements, either before or after you decided to cooperate, we don't see anything wherein those statements either you or Mr. Karadzic discussed or reminded each other about your previous conversation with respect to the principle of Western Slavonia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying nobody was able to hear that? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that from what I see here -- what I hear here, you have never stated that during that conversation President Karadzic reminded me of our conversation or hinted about, well, what are you going to do? Remember what we talked about, you know, somewhat in code. But there was nothing in that conversation that gave you any indication that President Karadzic was discussing the principle of Western Slavonia, such as you knew it to be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nothing was mentioned in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it -- because if we are to believe, okay, and I'm a skeptic, I must admit. I can't help that. But if we are to believe that this conversation did, in fact, take place on the 9th or the 8th, whatever, in Pale with respect to Western Slavonia, you indicate that it is President Karadzic who is asking you, in the plural, what you intend to do. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's during this conversation, if we are to believe what you said, that is during this conversation you tell President Karadzic that you are not in a position to speculate, because --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- After all there had been many occasions where there were attacks on Srebrenica and they never came to fruition. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course you've testified, and if we are to believe your testimony, this in fact was the first time that you had learned that there was even a possibility or one of the options was the actual taking over of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on the 11th when you called him, I take it from reading what I have here, and there's lots of material, perhaps too much, there is no indication that you, Deronjic, president of the SDS of Bratunac who now was in the position to answer that question to President Karadzic with respect to what should happen to the people and whether the principle of Western Slavonia should be instituted, you never raised that with the president either, did you? At least we don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand whether that was a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that a yes or a no for the interpreters, it wasn't clear. I took it as a no.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, if I understand your testimony, even today it seems to me that you were left with the impression that those that were to be separated were to be classified as or identified and classified as individuals who had committed war crimes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, your understanding was that there was not to be an indiscriminate separation of everyone of military age, which would be from 15 or 16 to 60, but rather there would be some sort of a selection process, where if people were known to have committed crimes, war crimes, they would be put aside, and of course they would be titled prisoners of war and treated accordingly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to that method, absolutely I agree. Yes, that's what was the idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to a statement. It's a misstatement of the fact. There's nothing in the record to indicate that 15 years old is an age that is of military age in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but 16 years is also mentioned. So should we stick to 16 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 16 to 60 is the military age, although the Prosecution, I believe, in the past has indicated that there had been some 15 year-olds that -- and I didn't want to draw any objection that I was mischaracterising, but I take the position and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At some point on the 12th you had learned from Mr. Vasic, who you knew and got along with, that there was some separation going, and you asked him to instruct or pass along your wishes, since you were in no position to order, but your wishes to General Mladic that that was to stop, the separation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on that same day, on that same day, the 12th of July, you were also holding a meeting, sort of a rally, were you not, in the town of Bratunac for the people of Bratunac, or certain people of -- certain citizens who perhaps would be going back to Srebrenica, because they were there in Bratunac as refugees. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, you spent a great deal of energy and time preparing for that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much energy and time as I had to spend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I understand the situation as it was occurring, you were the only one that actually addressed the crowd as the new commissioner of Srebrenica, having been vested this power from the President. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, preparations begun, you know, for the eventuality of the moving of these people back to Srebrenica, and perhaps the first task was the setting up of a police station there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I understand the situation as it was occurring back then, you were in close consultation with your closest associates?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, you have said as much about who these close -- your closest associates were. And I believe - I want to make sure I get them right - Mr. Simic, who was president of the municipality; Mr. Davidovic; Mr. Vasic; Mr. Borovcanin; and others. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so I take it, from what you have given -- this is from one of your statements, you viewed Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovcanin as close associates or your closest associates, one of your closest associates? At least that's what you say here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I did not say the closest associates. It's true to say that I knew them. Mr. Borovcanin was for a while in Bratunac as the commander of the police. And Vasic I know from Zvornik. Where does it say that they were my closest associates, Vasic and Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Since you ask, let me help you out this here. And this is from your testimony or your -- the statement that you gave on June 18th, 2003. It's --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you said -- you said I'm constantly thinking of the text that I have in front of me -- well, go ahead and read what you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me read what it says. I have the English version; it's on page 34. And I'm reading from lines 31 onwards. "Yesterday we finished the interview at the" -- this is you speaking. "Yesterday we finished the interview at the point when I described the end of the meeting, which was in fact a public discussion, a public forum held in the cinema building, following which I went to the SDS premises. In addition to myself, others came with me to the SDS premises. Those were my closest associates. Mr. Simic, who was the president of the municipality; Mr. Davidovic; Vasic; Borovcanin; and other people that I mentioned yesterday."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you're talking about semantics, but this is also a part of that. But this is as long ago as 1998. But you can also interpret it in that or in this way. Let me tell you who my closest associates were. Vasic, Simic -- Simic, Davidovic, and Vasic, and Borovcanin. I could have added others, too, but that does not have to mean that all of the persons named were my closest associates, if you want to analyse it like that. But let's not go into semantics again. I agree, I knew these people, I knew Borovcanin. I even considered him to be a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you had lobbied President Karadzic to bring him, who was a MUP, to bring him up there for the campaign of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- this has been gone over constantly, the relationship he's had, we've talked about boyhood friends. I think he said that he recommended Borovcanin to go five, six times. This is a lot of repetition. In fact most of this morning has been repetition. I haven't objected. But I don't see why there's any need to constantly repeat things. If -- it's inflaming the situation, too, because as you see it breaks down into arguments. These old arguments of yesterday and the day before are brought up again and they're more difficult when you have them a second and third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we don't think the matter of the closest associates is that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is a point. I can understand the Prosecutor wishing to hide the truth, because Borovcanin was charged. They allowed him to escape, basically, escape from being here. He should be here. He was indicted. And I am trying to show a linkage, because my next question, had Mr. McCloskey allowed me to ask it, would have been: Isn't it a fact that you have stated to the Prosecution in those days Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Vasic were coming to you asking you to act as an intermediary between Mladic and them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request this Court at this time to ask Mr. Karnavas to try to restrain himself from these incredible accusations. I'm used to them by now, frankly but -- and I know he doesn't really mean them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's in my pleadings, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- he's doing the same thing to the witness repeatedly. It just inflames the situation. It doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the question you put to this witness is a relevant one. You may ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There is no necessity to bring the Prosecution into the picture in this context. Any conclusions should be drawn by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Prosecution accuses me of trying to inflame the situation, I need to remind them why I'm -- why, perhaps, they may be feeling some heat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just stick to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that during those days Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovcanin were coming to you and asking you to act as an intermediary between them and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer that question, but if I can only ask the Trial Chamber for a clarification because my lawyer isn't here now. Does Mr. Karnavas have the right really to say, the witness is feeling some heat? I know exactly what he means, but I don't see why he needs to speculate whether I'm feeling heat or not. And I too am getting used to it, but I really cannot take it all lying down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I believe that the -- Mr. Karnavas, the Defence counsel, has a right to ask the questions which are relevant to our case. But I agree with you, there's no necessity for Mr. Karnavas to add more words other than necessary. We have been used to it. I hope you don't mind about that. If that happens, I'll warn Mr. Karnavas once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, there was a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The heat was for the Prosecutor, not for you, sir. A wrong interpretation. All right, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. And in that case, I apologise to you. I will answer your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please answer the question so we can get going.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what part of my statement are you referring to? Is it in the last interview? In which paragraph so I can look it up and refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, while I'm looking it up, let me ask you this question: Mr. Borovcanin had advised you at some point, had he not, that he had heard that General Mladic was scheduled to leave for Zepa or the forces were scheduled to leave for Zepa on the 14th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the interpreter got it right. What I heard was something about Mladic leaving Zepa. I know what you mean. Ljubisa Borovcanin and I were discussing the decision, and the idea was for Mladic to move from Bratunac to Zepa or against Zepa. That was the decision of the 12th of July discussed by Mr. Borovcanin and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that decision concerned you, did it not, that Mladic would be going off towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm being told that perhaps there's a problem with the translation. Let me go back. You gave a statement to the Prosecution on the -- I believe this would have been the 19th of June, 2003. And I'm quoting from page 41, I'll go slowly, and let's see if this is correct. And I'll be reading from line 25. "Ljubo Borovcanin told me about Mladic having issued an order. I'm not exactly sure when, but military should move towards Zepa on 14th. That information was very significant for me and also very upsetting, if I may use that word. I thought that the" -- and it's a little unclear there. "I thought that the -- was no where near to be completed that the majority of the Muslim forces were not defeated and that Muslims were very close to the Bratunac area and that anything was possible. And another aspect of that that particularly upset me was the following one: What upset me was that we already knew that there were many Muslims imprisoned there in Bratunac. I told you that they were imprisoned in the school, the hangar, the stadium, and what occurred to me is that -- or rather, what it seemed to me at the time was that Mladic just wanted to distance himself from the whole problem and just leave with the military basically, cover himself -- the paperwork and let the civilian authorities, possibly police, be responsible for the faith" -- it should be fate -- "of the Muslim prisoners. I am not saying that I knew this for a fact. I'm just saying that it occurred to me. I had this impression. Perhaps that was not justified, but this is something that made me quite concerned. And then I talked to Ljubisa Borovcanin regarding that, and he agreed with me to a great extent. He was also concerned that he and his police would be involved." Now, do you recall making this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Karnavas. And let us note one thing. You keep saying that my earlier statements are absolutely untrue, and now you have stated word for word something from my earlier statement, and let us note that this for once is absolutely true. In response to a previous question of yours when you asked me whether that decision had anything to do with me, I replied no, because I meant I was not going to move to Zepa myself or anything like that. But if you mean whether it concerned me indirectly and whether I had any thoughts about it like what it could possibly mean, then the answer is yes. And I described here what exactly that decision meant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps, as I said, there was a miscommunication with the translation. The fact that Mladic was leaving with the military while the prisoners were still in Bratunac, that was your concern. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because the civilian authorities, MUP, your close -- one of your closest associates, Borovcanin and Vasic, would then have to also be responsible for the fate of those prisoners, what would happen to them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could become responsible. I'm not saying that they were not responsible as it is, but I had the impression that Mladic wants to leave the responsibility for the prisoners to civilian authorities and the police, which I thought inappropriate. And if that had indeed happened, maybe their fate would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it would have been, but that was your concern, that the military was leaving, the prisoners were there in schools, in warehouses, and you were going to have to deal with that situation. You and the civilian structure, including the local police and the special police, all members of the Ministry of Interior. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And while this is going on, you're at the same time holding these meetings with respect to what should occur to the people, the refugees, from Srebrenica that are -- the Serb refugees, that is, trying to get them back from Bratunac to Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did hold that meeting, but I don't know what you mean by saying while that is going on. What is going on on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let me clue you in. You have Potocari, which is only 5 kilometres away from Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we all know what's going on. I think the question is what Mr. Karnavas meant by that, and it appears Mr. Karnavas is now going to give us a rendition of what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to show, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think Mr. Karnavas is trying to explain to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have two scenarios being played out here. One is what's happening in Potocari; another one what is happening in Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you see it, maybe. Maybe you think these are two separate stories. That's not the way I see it. In any case, Mladic went to his office -- Mladic went to Potocari, and I went to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me go further. You were responsible, both to the people that were in Potocari and to the Serb refugees that were in Bratunac, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just tried to -- started to explain what was going on, and now you stopped. I cannot jump from subject to subject. Let us have a single context of discussion. I told you what the responsibilities were towards ones and the others. And then you give a lump sum qualification for everything in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While the people were being separated in Potocari, you were trying to cater to the Serb refugees in Bratunac, correct, by holding these rallies. And there was not just one meeting, but there were two.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are trying to say that I didn't do anything, and that's obvious in the way you are phrasing your questions. And you are leading me to give you a specific answer. What I said is that ignoring the scale at which people were being separated -- I didn't know, because Mladic was in Potocari with the entire elite of the VRS. I didn't have any reason to expect any wrong doing. And I had no information on what scale people were being separated in Potocari. At that time, I was holding a meeting conveying conclusions and discussion points from different meetings. I had no feeling, no premonition, that a tragedy was about to occur. Who says that on the 12th there were elements that could indicate to me that a tragedy was going to occur? I had a feeling that something bad was beginning to happen. At some point I got a report saying that that had stopped. I was happy with that. I thought that Mladic had seized those activities and didn't look into it any further. On the 13th when prisoners were brought to Bratunac in droves, I told you how I reacted. Let me not repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll get to the 13th. Perhaps -- I think it's time for the break, but during the break you can come up with an answer as to why you never went to Potocari. Okay? Think of that. Perhaps when we come back we can pick up from there. Why you never went to Potocari if you had this premonition and you had this mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, please tell us why you did not go to Potocari on the 12th or the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will answer your question. There are several reasons. Whenever you think I'd said enough, you can interrupt me. Reason one, I had agreed with Mr. Karadzic to keep him posted. I left Fontana, as I wrote in my report to my office, to call him and inform him of the course of the meeting and what we had accomplished at the Fontana Hotel. I explained that at length already. I won't repeat that, to save time. Reason two, based on the orders issued by Mladic and the tasks issued to everyone as we were leaving, I understood that the order, as pertaining to civilian authorities, primarily people from the municipality because he didn't mention me specifically, was to secure a certain amount of food and water for the people who were held in Potocari because the humanitarian situation was critical, as was noted at the meeting. And to make sure, as far as we were able, that enough vehicles for transport were secured. So I went to the office to work on that, because I knew a lot of people in the community who were able to help us. Just for example, bread, a certain amount of bread, was delivered from Zvornik at my request after I called President Simic. We called up Ljubovija and various other municipalities to take care of the various tasks that Mladic had given us. Another one, General Mladic with his entire entourage, his topmost associates and representatives of the UNPROFOR with their vehicles went to Potocari. I thought their presence was completely sufficient, and I didn't see any reason for myself to go there and waste time, because nobody at that point expected that something was going to deteriorate after the meeting. I had a good reason to believe it wouldn't, and that is that the command of the UNPROFOR had left the Fontana Hotel, together with General Mladic in a generally friendly atmosphere, and nobody asked me to go to Potocari with them. Nothing that happened during that day indicated that a drama was about to occur. I was supposed to continue with my regular duties and preparations for entering into Srebrenica. I informed President Karadzic about that, and I told him what my intentions were. He approved that and he told me to continue with my work and my preparations for that day. Do you need me to give you more reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That will be fine. Now, was it that same day -- I should say, was it not on that same day that you held a meeting at the small university conference room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the evening.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And That's a separate one from the one you had held earlier, the rally, I believe it was at the cinema. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I indicated -- as I understand the situation, there were convoys already moving that day, that afternoon, and that evening. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Very soon after the meeting, I don't know the exact hour, the first convoys set out from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were conducting your preparations for entering Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We were continuing those preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in essence, you were waiting for that evacuation or for the convoys to be -- to leave. So once that completed, you could then go into Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At one point I understand that you asked the civilian police to get on the megaphones and to call out the citizens, I believe that was for one of the meetings that you held in Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I apologise, Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood what you meant. I asked for that announcement to be made not only on the megaphones but also on the radio for citizens from Srebrenica to go to the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that on the 12th and 13th or just the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th because the meeting was held in the evening of the 12th, and there was no need for citizens to rally on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Suffice it to say that if someone was walking around Bratunac centre, they would have heard these megaphones?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to digress a little bit and go back to before your meeting with President Karadzic on the 8th or 9th. As I understand your testimony, you had been out in the field along with another individual during the campaign against Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that individual - his name escapes me right now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Glogovac, he was also from the civilian sector, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's under the Ministry of Interior. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so at that point in time as I understand it, you were unaware of what exactly the mission was on the attack of Srebrenica. You didn't know the goal?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood that quite well, and I have said it many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I find it rather curious - and perhaps you can explain -- give us some explanation as to how is it that if President Karadzic had problems with Mladic, why would he keep his top official, president of the SDS party, in the complete dark as to what the ultimate goal or goals of Srebrenica were, while at the same time inform the military.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very unusual question indeed, but I will answer. In that zone, countless military operations took place, some of them you mentioned and noted. It was true. Not for a single military operation in which various brigade commanders were involved was the civilian sector informed or the president of the party, because I suppose there are certain matters which are completely in the hands of the army alone. Why would the president of the SDS have to be aware of military objectives? You have to address that question to the relevant person. I wasn't told and I didn't think I should.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless, according to you, at some point you realised that you needed to find out, and that's why you went to Pale. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated a number of reasons for going to Pale, among other things, to find out -- not because I had to find out and not that there was any guarantee that I would be told. I simply wished to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, one of your concerns was the operation wasn't going well enough and that they needed serious assistance from someone that was from the Ministry of the Interior, from MUP, Mr. Borovcanin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, repetitive. This has all been gone over in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in the field, I understand it, you were able to come across General Krstic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was on the first day when I arrived, possibly the day after my arrival. I met with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And general -- and you didn't have any problems with General Krstic, not like, for instance, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any problems with him because I had no relationship whatsoever. It was the first time I laid my eyes on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you knew his position, did you not? You knew that he was the chief of staff of the Drina Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the particulars of who was what, but I did see him in command, commanding there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it -- and from what I understand, you went and introduced yourself to him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say it with some hesitancy. Isn't it a fact that you went there, introduced yourself, spoke to him, and perhaps - that's what you said, perhaps - had a cup of coffee with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say I hesitated, but we are talking about something that took place eight years ago. I don't believe that to be very relevant, but it's true, I did go up to him, I introduced myself, we spoke briefly, I don't remember whether there was coffee or not. It's quite possible. I know exactly where the table is where we sat at the forward command post, where the logistics building was. I had a friend there, a neighbour with whom I spoke. I cannot remember all the details, but if that's not so relevant, I don't know why you are insisting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you didn't ask General Krstic what was the ultimate aim on the attack of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point, I didn't have any dilemmas about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, before heading all the way 130 to 140 kilometres to Pale when you did have the dilemma, why not track down General Krstic who was at or around Pribicevac any during that period? Why go all the way to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained why. First of all, I met Krstic at one point, probably the first day when I arrived. I'm not claiming that 100 per cent, but it's correct 90 per cent. At that point, I assumed based on earlier information about Srebrenica, my talks with Karadzic on different occasions, that there was a major problem about Srebrenica, which I explained earlier, and that is the gap between our lines in the southern part. So we probably spoke about that. Nobody said that there were any deeper more important objectives. It was also important for me to spend a day or two on the lines. One night I slept with those men together in the trenches. I don't know exactly where that was, at Livnakja [phoen], for example. It was important to speak to those people, to toe the lines. My colleagues were there, the teachers from school, you know, at the time everybody was mobilised. A large number of people who didn't have a lot of experience in war, who were not in military operations too often. Such people were asking me different questions, hoping I would know the answer, what was going on. There was fighting already, there were casualties already. People were afraid. So I concluded - of course I had my own ideas about everything in that conversation - I concluded that it would be more logical to get explanations from the president since I didn't have any concrete duties there at the time. I'm not a soldier in the classic sense. I wasn't mobilised. It seemed to me that I was just wasting time there. It would be better for me to go to Pale to see what the objectives were of that action so that I could explain that to people. And it seemed to me that the operations at that point were becoming more complex, so that's the reason. Perhaps I could have asked Krstic also, but I don't know the man. I noticed that he had a lot of work to do. He was in command later, I didn't see him. He was out in the field for some time then he was back. I wasn't close to him in order to ask him. And ultimately perhaps such a high officer would not feel any need to explain anything to me. So these are all my views on it. Perhaps they're not absolutely right but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know Colonel Blagojevic at the time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You knew that he was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know the dates. I said that I wasn't following that -- the date of his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You knew at that time that he was the commander, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You knew at that time that he was from Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know at what point I found out that Mr. Blagojevic was born in Bratunac and that he had family there. It's possible I knew it at the time. I cannot remember when I found that out. I didn't know Mr. Blagojevic earlier. I didn't meet him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you think it would be logical for a commander to be concerned about the well being of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you never spoke with Mr. Blagojevic to find out what the plan was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that he did not have the same position and exude the same sort of power as Mladic, Krstic, or even Zivanovic, for whom you had very little taste for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with your statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while you were at the field, you also came across - I believe he was a lieutenant colonel at the time - Pandurevic. He might have been a colonel, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember the rank. I didn't come across him. But I went to actually see that action up close. I went to the actual location where he was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And -- but you even had an opportunity to speak with him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I just greeted him like this. I can describe it. He was -- it's a trench in the left part of Pribicevac, and from that trench which was being fired on, there was firing -- so we were in that trench. I just said hello to him. He was issuing orders as far as I can remember. I could see that with my eyes. That unit was in the process of taking an elevation, so I followed that for a few minutes. And I understand that it wasn't my place to be there absolutely, that I was just in the way as fighting was going on, so I withdrew. There was firing. I think at the time they had a couple of wounded, a couple of Legenda's soldiers were hurt. I heard that over the radio. But the situation wasn't really suitable to discuss anything like that. Before that, I asked Pandurevic -- I saw him once or twice. I saw him once in 1992. And once in 1993, I just remembered, in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In reading your statements and transcripts, one gets the appearance that perhaps it was during the efforts that were being made by Pandurevic and Legenda of the Drina Wolves that led you to the firm conviction that a serious military unit needed to be brought into the area.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the information that I gathered over those few days, including what you are talking about, made me think, amongst other things, that perhaps a more professional unit needed to be there. My primary objective was to try to protect those people, my neighbours. Bratunac is a small town. Everybody knows everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the more professional unit that you had in mind was from the civilian sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the same area that's been gone over and over and over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm about to put the next question. I need that answer, Your Honour. I know it's been gone over. I'd like the answer so I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you can put your question more specifically. What do you mean by the civilian sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Isn't it, isn't it -- can we not draw a logical conclusion, Mr. Deronjic, that the reasons you went to see President Karadzic in order to lobby for MUP, and in particular Mr. Borovcanin, was so that you could maintain control over the situation after the fall of Srebrenica, because by the time you went there it was obvious to everyone that Srebrenica was about to fall?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't don't understand. First of all, I said I didn't know that they would enter Srebrenica. At that point, I drew some conclusions. What do you mean control over Srebrenica? What sort of control over Srebrenica am I supposed to have? It's unclear. I'm really trying to help you, but I don't understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question or one similar to it was asked and dealt with yesterday. Mr. Deronjic had answered extensive questions about his ability to control the special police and these other issues. So this is in effect a rehash of material again already gone over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But at this place, I believe that Mr. Karnavas is asking a question about the purpose of Mr. Deronjic to see the president. Am I right, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I replied to the question of what the purpose was. What I wanted was for that unit to come there and for me to find out what the real intentions regarding Srebrenica were and to consult about it all with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. In other words, you were not asking for another military unit to come from some other place of the Republika Srpska, you were asking for a specific unit that was attached or part of the Ministry of Interior. And you were asking for a particular individual who was from Bratunac or had been the chief of police of Bratunac, who you later on have described as one of your closest associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's been asked and answered several times and it -- it's fundamentally, I think, an unfair practice to deal with one subject one day, come to the same subject the next day when you've already gone through it and keep beating on it. The witness eventually crumbles sometimes. We've seen that happen. But not only is it asked and answered but it really is an unfair practice to go over the same topics over and over again. I don't have any problem with new directions or new twists, or new information, that's fine. But this is the same. I don't see any difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite understand your objection, Mr. McCloskey, but I believe that first this matter is actually important in this case. Secondly, Mr. Karnavas somehow changed a little bit from a different angle. So I think this question is allowed, but at the same time, Mr. Karnavas, don't try to travel on the repeated road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you give us an explanation why it is that you didn't ask for another military unit, as opposed to asking for your friend, your associate, who was from the civilian sector to come with his forces who were part of the Ministry of Interior. Can you give us an explanation, particularly in light of your observations that - and as you put it - a serious military unit needed to be there and you were concerned for the well being of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You've already mentioned some of the reasons. You said I knew Mr. Borovcanin, I knew that unit, I knew its structure. I had a lot of information about how much training it had had, how many times it had participated in the different fronts, and it had shown itself to be a very good unit in the military sense. All of these are reasons which made me decide. And anyway, as opposed to the military, which mostly used untrained people for different reasons - I'm not accusing them but that was the situation - and the lack of trained elite units, I believe that that resulted in much -- many losses on our side in unnecessary casualties. We often discussed this matter in the party and at higher levels as well about the need to form such a unit, to form a special brigade. But I don't want to deal with that too long. Anyway, up until 1995, Bratunac had over 1.000 casualties. I'm speaking about that entire area. I'm speaking about the people from Srebrenica who were there, Skelani is included, too. I explained how much -- this is over 10 per cent of the total Serb population in Bratunac. So all of these are reasons why I wanted to have a trained unit come. The only one I knew at the time was this special unit, which very often took part in actions on the front in less problematic assignments. And in particularly, Borovcanin was well familiar with the terrain around Bratunac. He was there on several occasions. So it did not seem logical to me that he wasn't there with his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It also seemed logical that he would be one that you could control?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question -- the assertion is not correct. My relations with the ministry for internal affairs with Mr. Kovac, if you ask me and if I'm permitted, I'm thinking about the Trial Chamber, I will explain to you what Tomislav Kovac's relationship was to me so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking for Kovac, I'm asking for Borovcanin. You did not call for Kovac --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, that's very argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like the witness, Your Honour, to answer the question. He wanted Borovcanin because he could control Borovcanin, he could work with Borovcanin. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it not, Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can briefly state, I'm sure we all remember the 10 July document ordering Mr. Borovcanin to the area. It's authored by Mr. Kovac. So I don't know what the answer to his question is, but my guess is his ability to control Mr. Borovcanin may have something to do with his comments about Mr. Kovac, who is Mr. Borovcanin's boss. So I think it's a fair answer that Mr. Karnavas should allow the witness to explain his answer, whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, the relationship with Kovac is irrelevant because Kovac has a particular duty. Once he gets an order from the president, that order -- then he must execute that order irrespective of whether he likes this gentleman or not. And then from Kovac the order comes down to Borovcanin. So in essence because this gentleman here had such pull with Karadzic, which he explains repeatedly in the statements, he was able to get President Karadzic to order Kovac to bring his particular man, Borovcanin, on the scene. That's what I'm alluding to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, please answer the question as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At no point, particularly during war operations, was I able to use any kind of power that you ascribe to me in order to be able to control a brigade whose commander, the true commander, of that brigade was Goran Saric whose commander I practically didn't know. He was the one who directly issued orders to Borovcanin. And Borovcanin was the chief of staff of the special brigade at the police. This was a very tightly -- tight unit, tightly interconnected to the chain of command, particularly during military operations, combat operations. So I hardly think that I could have any influence on the behaviour of that unit, and in particular, Mr. Borovcanin who was the commander of that unit, who was with that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's go to the events of July 13th. At some point it becomes obvious to you that the situation in Bratunac town is rather serious, safety-wise. Correct?
