utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for the record, was that based on observations, or was that based on someone coming to your office having to tell you this information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described that already. In order not to repeat that, information was conveyed to me from out in the field and from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So somebody had to come into your office, the SDS office, to tell you that the situation in Bratunac is rather vicarious?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say to the office. Perhaps to the office as well. I explained all the things that I did not course of the 13th, so it's possible that during a meeting which we held in the small conference room of the university -- it's possible at any point. People were coming in and out and they were informing us if the situation was dramatic. A meeting was not so important in the course of the operations to take Srebrenica, so that Davidovic, Vasic, Simic would not be able to enter to the meeting to inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at some point, you were urged, as I understand it, or you may have come to the realisation on your own, that you should contact President Karadzic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the 13th, towards the evening. If I have correct information, this conversation took place at 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And as you came to learn at some point accidentally, as you put it, that there was an intercept of that conversation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course I found out about it for the first time when this was shown to me in Belgrade, that transcript of the intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's a rather short conversation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not a transcript of a complete conversation. There are some parts of the conversation which were not recorded, and some of them -- over some, you can hear the sound of the teleprinter. So this is -- it's not a complete conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were able, through the Office of the Prosecution, to hear the recording of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw the transcript and it states there inaudible because of the noise of the teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the blanks, there's three dots, so it's your assumption that that's where this supposed conversation that wasn't recorded would have been?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there. Perhaps there are other breaks. I didn't go into it in the technical sense of all the things that are missing, but I assume the three dots would indicate what you say they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it rather coincidental that the most damning information against President Karadzic and others just happens to be in that blank information, the three dots?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we were to look at this intercept, there is nothing here about somebody coming with instructions, is there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part where he says that a man with instructions will come, it's missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's assuming that was said, because we have nothing to verify it, other than you, at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have. I don't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's my whole point. We have to trust Deronjic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we know that Deronjic has not always been truthful in the past, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in one of your previous interviews, this is before you were indicted, of course, you indicated that after you came back from this call with President Karadzic, you found Colonel Beara in your office. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall. But that is not correct. Colonel Beara came the way I said that, the way I explained that in my last interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just -- I want to cover this interview first, and we'll get to the last interview. In this interview you state that when you got to your office he was waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we just get an indication, I'm sorry, of which interview that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the interview is on 21 October, 1999. It's marked for identification purposes as P692, and I am referring to page 15. And the appropriate sections are around line 4. I'm told that this is marked for identification purposes as D95. I don't want to confuse anyone. And in the Srpski version, it's lines 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You said -- in this particular interview, you said that Karadzic -- you say: "Well, Karadzic told me that he's going to convey that information to General Mladic and that night Beara got into my office. Actually, he was waiting for me in my office. And because I was not present, the president of the municipality was sitting with him when I got there."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all correct, except for the fact that he was waiting for me. He came later, and I said at what time he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, can I ask why would you state that he was actually waiting for you, and the time would have been around 8.30 or so, given that the conversation with President Karadzic was around 8.00. How could you make such a mistake, or was this another one of your fabrications?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I fabricate something like that? There's no reason why I would. I was just describing that he was in my office, and I always tell the Prosecution at the outset at every interview that I'm not sure about dates, hours, details. I had no intention of concealing the fact that he was there. Does the way in which Beara appeared really matter at all? I described many times how he came, and we are not still certain after many statements when exactly he came, at what time, an hour less or more. Does it really matter? And if you look at my interviews, you will see that in every meeting I tell the Prosecution, I have no way of checking this. I have no way of verifying the details. I think that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, in this one instance you had one way of verifying it, and that would have been with the president of the municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But unfortunately Mr. Simic does not remember the chronology either. There are other people, my secretary, Mr. Sofir and others. Everyone remembers that Beara came, but they don't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Having stated that I want to go back into this interview to the previous page. And you indicate on page 14. And I'm reading from lines 19 to 26. You stated that: "Mr. Karadzic told me that all prisoners of war should be transported out of Bratunac. He was trying to tell me that in code, actually because that was an open-line conversation."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then you go on to say, he said that actually the "goods should be in the warehouse," that's verbatim, word for word of what he said, "and I got it as a 'military prison,' I got it on that way, that that was the military prison. And he told me that he was going to inform General Mladic to do it that way, because I told you the same situation in Bratunac at the time was very dramatic. That -- actually the president of the municipality had made an intervention with me as well as the president of the Executive Board. But they opposed to the fact that these people were to be held in civilian facilities. That is why I did it that way, I acted that way. So Karadzic told me that he is going to convey that information to General Mladic, and that night, you know, Beara got into my office," and then I quoted the rest. Now, if we look at this --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I just want to note that what you are reading differs, perhaps not significantly but in details from the original. Maybe it's a question of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, for that you will have to blame the Prosecutor, not me. This is an official translation that I have gotten from them. But if you think something is significant, you can point it out. But the essence of it is that Karadzic here, according to you, is telling you that he's going to give instructions to Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. But in my experience there's sometimes focus on single words. Please ask your question and if what you said here does not really matter in terms of particular words, then I will simply answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, is it not a fact that on 21 October 1999 you told the Prosecution that Karadzic -- President Karadzic had told you that he would be informing General Mladic to do it that way, that is to send these folks to a military prison, as you understood the coded words to be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you said that statement, we know for a fact at least, because we have the intercept, assuming the intercept is correct, that the quote with respect to the warehouse is approximately right on target. Because the intercept states: "All the goods must be placed inside the warehouse before 12.00 tomorrow." And you quote: "The goods should go to the warehouse." So that we can accept as being rather accurate. And of course we don't have --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked a question, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, is that accurate or not over all, the context of it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I haven't answered the question. It was a question and I want to answer it. You asked: Is that correct? And without letting me answer, you move on to another question. If you don't need my answer, I'm not going to give it. So at that moment when I was giving that statement, I was speaking to the best of my recollection. When I saw that transcript, I noticed that there is a discrepancy between what I said and certain parts that are missing, if the transcript is true. I am not trying to convince you of the truthfulness of my statement. But in 1997 and in 1998, I was describing that conversation. And when I testified later, and the transcript is available, you say that it's right on target. Wouldn't it be logical for you to accept that even the other parts of my statement are true, just if we rely on analogy. I asked the Prosecution to measure if there are there are lapses and how long they are in the intercepts. They told me they would do that. They said that the intercept is not continuous, there are breaks, and the transcript would reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the Prosecution told you that there was a gap there, probably, given the dots. And that at least gave you an indication that there might have been something that you didn't put in -- that wasn't in there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last one, yes. I'm not saying that you have to believe me. I'm just saying what we were able to note so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well, we're going step by step, Mr. Deronjic. Now, based on your answer, can we not then logically state or conclude that the remainder portion, that is, that President Karadzic was going to instruct General Mladic to take those prisoners out of Bratunac and to Batkovici or to some military prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained this to the Prosecution. I'm answering your question. I said that as far as this fact is concerned, I can really not claim with absolute certainty anything, as I wasn't able to claim anything about the arrival or the timing of the arrival of Mr. Beara. And I cannot really speak in this instance of something that I am not absolutely sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Then if we extend that by analogy, later on when you have your deal from the Prosecution and then you come up with the -- you fill in the blanks where you say President Karadzic tells you he's going to send someone with instructions, can we not also state that you're not sure that that's what was said either to you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not fair to say that I made a deal and then gave an interview. I gave an interview before I made the deal. You can see my interview with Mr. Harmon submitted as part of my case where it says: Mr. Deronjic undertook to give truthful statements and cooperate substantially without any promises, and so on and so forth. So my interview has nothing to do with the deal. That's the first fact that I want cleared up. Second, I claim that there is evidence for everything I stated, at least for 99 per cent of what I said there is evidence. Of course you will always ferret out something, a minor part, for which evidence is hard to find. But I didn't stage any of this. It is very difficult for me to organise evidence which doesn't exist. But if you take the bulk of my statements, for every detail you can challenge me and I will find you evidence to prove it. You cannot say that everything is untrue, everything that I said. Mr. Karnavas, after all it is an undisputable fact that Mr. Beara came to my office after my conversation with the president. That does not mean anything in itself, but it lends plausibility to what I stated. I agree with you that it is not fool-proof evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Since you mentioned that, just to get the points out in the open, when Colonel Beara came and he said that he had orders from the top, as you have stated, you never asked him concretely: Are those orders from President Karadzic, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about. I didn't ask the question directly. I just said, Mr. Beara, I don't have any such orders. I did talk to President Karadzic and I have orders of a different kind. But I didn't ask the question in so many words. I had the conversation I had with Karadzic. After that, I received the visit of this gentleman, and I put two and two together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me put the question again, sir. You never asked him who the top is because he is in the military structure and his top could be number one, right, Mladic? Your top was another number one, that's Karadzic. Did you ask for clarification what he meant when he said he has orders from the top, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the tone and the elevated voice. It's going to -- that's argumentative; it's not going to get us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but the question itself has some meanings in it. So I hope the witness could answer that question. I also warn Mr. Karnavas, be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you, but let me explain to the Honorable Trial Chamber, there is no need to interrupt us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I object. I ask him a pointed question, yes or no. He should answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, please answer the question directly. If you feel you need some explanation, and then you could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to give a clarification, but I'll skip it. Mr. Karnavas, I think you digress sometimes, perhaps deliberately, and I have to come back to the subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object again. There's no answer here. I put a specific question to the witness, yes or no, did he ask for clarification as to who the top was. I would like a clear answer. He's dancing around the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, I have already given you instructions how to approach this issue. Answer the question first. If you feel you need, you may give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is no, I didn't ask him that. But what I want to say is this: You suggested this on a number of occasions, that it was never -- I never asked him. I never met the man again. How could I ask him? Between Mladic and Karadzic, there was no disagreement as to the military operation. In the war, Mr. Karadzic is the supreme commander of the armed forces. In my eyes at that moment, it was not so important whether the order was issued by Karadzic or Mladic. What is the big difference? I didn't feel that as an important distinction. I didn't ask him. He just said: I have orders from the top. And he obviously wanted to keep it discreet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Allow me to point out the distinction. Here comes a man who wants to kill innocent people. You have a particular order, as you state. As a human being, as the head of the party, as the most powerful man in Bratunac with a mandate, did you not think that it might be relevant to say: Who gave you such an inhumane barbaric order that you're going to kill 7.000 people or 2.000 people, or 1.000, whatever the number was? Did it ever occur to you to ask: How could you dare do such a thing? Who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, I had a more important priority. My first priority is to prevent Mr. Beara -- please do not make faces at me. I am not making faces when you are being unduly pathetic. My first priority was to prevent Mr. Beara to put this all in practice. That was a much more important task. Discussions were continuing in an atmosphere which was already largely disrupted. I told you that I had to make a person leave the room because I didn't want him to hear the conversation. I wanted to spare him from the knowledge that our leaders could even be contemplating such orders. So I remained one-on-one with Mr. Beara. That first night I rang for security around those people, and I already had in place in agreement, which I maybe didn't mention because that's part of my defence. I cautioned Mr. Beara that I was going to see the president in the morning and to convey to him our conversation. There were a lot of other things said, not all of which I described, but I described the essence, perhaps not word for word because it was eight years ago. But a lot of things were said, with people coming and going all the time. In the morning I went to see the president. I managed to forestall that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you saw the president the next day, did you concretely and directly ask the president whether Beara was the one that he had ordered to come and grab or take the prisoners out of there so he could kill them or have them killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to Karadzic, word for word, Mr. Beara came to my office, told me this and this. I didn't ask the question -- I didn't put it the way you put it. I put it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ask him directly: Mr. President, yesterday when you told me on this intercept that you would be sending somebody with instructions, was that be any chance this Colonel Beara who came and told me that he was there to kill all of the prisoners? Did you tell him that? Did you ask him that question, yes or no, directly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that directly. We discussed the situation, and I had an opportunity to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why didn't you ask him directly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Beara didn't say I got orders from Mr. Karadzic. He said I got orders from the top. That's one. Second, he was drunk, very drunk. I didn't have the freedom to ask Karadzic, Look, Mr. President, did you order the killing of 7.000 people? And I had my doubts about Beara. The way I put my question was such that Karadzic had to tell me in no uncertain terms whether it was true or not. There was no ambiguity. He had to give me a clear answer, and he had to tell me what he thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, could it be that your conversation with Beara was that you do not care about whether those people who you were supposed to protect were killed; it's just that you did not want them killed in Bratunac. Isn't that another logical conclusion that we can draw, based on what you're saying and what you have said and under the circumstances as they existed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was my first priority, to prevent it from happening until we clear up the situation, to prevent it from happening ever. And we have records of that. We have five years of statements and interviews. I never uttered that it was acceptable for me that these people be killed. Maybe one day I will be indicted too and we'll have an opportunity to clarify it further. So far I haven't presented my defence, and there is no need for us to discuss what I thought, what I intended, et cetera. It would sound demagogical and I don't want to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Needless to say, on that night, the 13th, you didn't go back to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to get on the phone and to try to contact President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, I finished my meeting at 3.00 a.m. That's what I always said in my working interviews. In Nikolic's statement you can read that it was over around 12.00. In any case, we continued our preparations. And I don't know exactly when I went home, but it was in the small hours of the next day, with the knowledge that I was going to Pale the next day. I hope I answered your question. How was I supposed to call up the president at 3.00 a.m. Or 4.00 a.m.? He's not sitting in his office all the time. He has to sleep sometime, too. I did secure the agreement that I would see him, and I did secure -- I did make sure that nothing would happen that night. And as for the rest, I would go and see him tomorrow. That's what I was thinking at the time. That was logical I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you could go at any point in time to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to use their communication facilities as you wished. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't need, for instance, permission from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, you had the authority to go and use those communication means, which were supposed to be secure especially when having sensitive conversations with the president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Absolutely correct. I just want to add, I always asked for permission, because that's the kind of man I am, although I didn't strictly need to. They would always tell me, of course, go on and call.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say "permission." You never asked permission from Colonel Blagojevic directly. You didn't go to his office and say, Colonel, Commander, I need to use the communications?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. I would rather go to the brigade and contact the duty officer. Mr. Blagojevic wasn't around in those days. I would ask the duty officer who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to recap, you had a very inebriated individual who, as you had indicated, you had met for the first time. He was speaking in a rather bizarre manner to the point where he was openly saying that he was there to kill all of the prisoners. Correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, he was so brazen about what he wanted to do that -- and he was speaking to openly, that it caused you concern, hence you taking your close associate and friend out of that room, Mr. Simic, so he would not be subjected to this conversation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but at that point the conversation began on that topic right then; the conversation didn't really proceed too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. He leaves. Now it's you and it's Beara. And as I understand it, you put a little fuel to the fire because when Beara wanted another drink, you provided him with some vodka, at least that's what you said in some of your statements. You had sort of a drink, which is customary, at least in that part of the world, anyway. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Let me answer the question first and then give the explanation. You said I was pouring oil on to the fire, as if at that moment I knew why Beara had come and I wanted to make him more angry with the alcohol. It's not like that. A high officer came, I offered him a drink. He said -- yes, I noticed this that he was slightly inebriated, but that is a custom of ours to offer a drink or coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, coffee might have been a little more appropriate under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not the one who makes that decision. I acted according to his wishes. I agree with you. It would have better had he not have come at all, now that we're talking about what would have been best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have our coffee break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm about to close on this issue. Why does Mr. McCloskey have to be so rude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I think the mention of coffee triggered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He see's me, Your Honour, he sees me looking at the clock. I'm well aware of it. I'm just about to close on the issue, and now he wants to break. And this is done routinely in the United States as a way of breaking the thread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's finish, let's finish this action first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. If we can close, I can sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during this period you learn that this madman wants to kill, you know, a large amount of people, don't you think that if you wanted to contact President Karadzic, even at 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning, just to be on the safe side, that you could have got a hold of President Karadzic. Don't you think that would have been possible?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are several reasons for that and I will list them all. One of the reasons why I didn't call I already mentioned. I know for sure that at that time he's not at the presidency. I would have to look for him privately. I don't know where he lived when he's at Pale. I've never seen him there. I agree, I should speak up -- I don't even know the telephone. This is what I'm trying to say. Secondly, in a previous conversation between myself and Karadzic he warned me, and you have that in the transcript, it says: If you have anything confidential, and this is the most confidential kind of information, don't do it by telephone, send it by teleprinter or in some other way through more secure communications. This is that kind of information which I wouldn't even dare to send over the teleprinter. I didn't know if it was true. Of course it could prove to be very dangerous. At the brigade command it seemed to me pointless to go there at that time. It didn't seem to be much point in going to there and calling from there because the next day I was going to Pale anyway. And I would have gone early, had I not been delayed by the Ciglani event. So I went there two or three hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in one of your statements - I'm referring to 12 March 2001 - you were asked whether you knew what instructions Mr. Beara had. And you indicated back then that you did not know. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when -- and that statement, I take it, given your testimony here today or for the past several days, that statement was false at the time it was made?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in order for us to accept your version of events with respect to what transpired during that telephone conversation with President Karadzic, we would have to accept your word for it, would we not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other things, I don't know what else you or the Prosecution have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, concretely, we don't have that tape with -- where you're speaking. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have it -- I don't know if you have it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you were never provided with a tape-recording by the Prosecution of your conversation with Mr. Karadzic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was no one else that was -- that gave a statement that we know of or that you looked at where they have indicated that in fact President Karadzic had said: I will be sending someone with instructions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, whether anybody made a statement regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Assuming that there are no statements, because there aren't any to my knowledge, then all we would have left is your word and your word alone, save for if we had President Karadzic over here or the former President Karadzic over here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And even if we did have President Karadzic here, if he were to say, No, I never said that, then you would maintain that this is what he said, at this point we would have a dilemma which of the two we should believe, President Karadzic or you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand and as we talked a little bit about it, over the years as the case against you or the investigation, I should say, against you progressed from you being a witness to a suspect, during this period of time you were conducting your own investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the degree I described, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were looking for documents that might be of some assistance in at least giving you some clues as to what might be in the possession of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was checking it orally more. I of course could not look for documents on the assumption that nobody would give them to me anyway. If you're thinking of any documents of your own or the possibility that I made some notes, wrote some things down, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact -- at least we know with respect to the chronology, you consulted a certain friendly connections that we talked about yesterday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair for us to assume that including the names that we mentioned yesterday, we should also include some of your closest associates at the time, that is Mr. Vasic and Mr. Borovcanin, did you not consult them as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember one occasion with Vasic and I remember one occasion with Borovcanin when we discussed this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When was it that you met with Mr. Borovcanin, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to Bratunac once. We met. After an indictment was issued against him or perhaps there was some indications of that, I'm not quite sure about that, we met briefly and talked about this topic in a cafe or restaurant called Jasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that would have been in the last year or two?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that. I've been here for almost two years, so it could have been -- yes, before that. I really couldn't tell you exactly when it was. I remember that he was coming back from a vacation. He was on a vacation and he dropped by in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But was that before or after, say, 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say that it was after 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if you had told the Office of the Prosecution as late as 8 April 2002 that you hadn't seen Mr. Borovcanin for at least three or four years, that would have been false, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year did I state that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This would have been on -- actually, I believe it's the 9th April 2002, and I'm quoting from page 146 of the transcript that was provided to us of your statement given in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I probably said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you had probably said that -- well, actually you did say it. And so since you did say it, that was false information, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Borovcanin had already been indicted [Realtime transcript read in error "invited"]. So if I am linked with him, then there would be assumptions that I knew where he was. And I had enough trouble as it is without that, or perhaps at that point I did not remember that we had talked. But I do not want to give you any other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The transcript should read "indicted" as opposed to "invited," I understand. So you wanted to protect yourself, and so in order to protect yourself you provided the Office of the Prosecution with false information.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? I'm protecting Borovcanin more than myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, sir, they ask you a concrete question and then you state that you haven't seen Mr. Borovcanin, who you -- we've already discussed is one of your closest associates at that period of time, the critical period. And you indicate that you haven't seen him for three or four years. Thus, one would conclude that you had no contact with him, hence no ability to get together with him to sort of discuss the events and maybe have a unified front on the events, the facts, the dates, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether -- I am responding the question. Whether I spoke to Borovcanin or not has nothing to do with the events the Srebrenica; it's not relevant. Has it ever happened to you in life that you remember something later. You're walking down the street and you go "Aha, I remember something." Is it possible for you to remember something at one point and not another point? If you need, I can provide you a scientific explanation about why this happens. For example, in a whole variety of events in which you took part you forget one fact. It seems as if it never happened to you. But then later you might be walking down the street, you might have an association, and then you would go "Aha" and remember something that happened to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the question that was posed to you by Mark Harmon is, and I'm reading from page 146, it's paragraph 25.1. It says: "Did Mr. Borovcanin, who was in charge of the special police ever conduct an investigation into the crime at Kravica warehouse? "A. I haven't seen Mr. Borovcanin for at least three or four years. I know that currently he is in Banja Luka. I don't know telephone number, and he is not really calling me, so I cannot answer this question. He is very unwilling to have contacts with anybody regarding these events."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I did say that. He was not willing. He didn't even give me his phone number or anything. We just happened to meet accidentally in the middle of the street. He was coming out of his car, so he couldn't avoid me. It's well-known that for a number of years Borovcanin is not in that area. I'm not going to go into is the reasons, but basically nobody knows where he's living and working for a long number of years. At that point, perhaps I didn't remember. I don't want to go into further details. I didn't remember that I had seen him. But this wasn't an investigation. We were not conducting an investigation; we were just talking about events. What I said later, this happened on the 13th when he told me about it, but this wasn't an investigation. He just told me about the incident relating to Kravica. But afterwards later, we didn't discuss that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless you would agree with us that this is incorrect information. Intentional, unintentional, it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I just want to add an explanation. Mr. Borovcanin told me on that occasion that the Prosecution -- that he admitted that information to the Prosecution that he was there, that he saw and was around during those conversations regarding Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Speaking of Kravica, is not Kravica within the Bratunac municipality, you know, the general area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would that not be under your purview, your powers, your domain as the president of the SDS for the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you wish de jure, no, because I had a different function than for Srebrenica. Kravica does not belong to Srebrenica de facto or de jure. But I want to say that this did happen in Bratunac and I was in Bratunac. Are you asking me if I have any information about that? Yes, then these answers are correct. I'm not avoiding any questions, but de jure, I'm not. Since sometimes you are talking about de jure and de facto. I am saying de jure, I am not. So let us note that. As for de facto ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as you indicated, and I don't have the exact quote but I can dig it out, that sometimes de facto can be much more powerful than de jure -- one's powers can be much more meaningful. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. We will go back to that question of powers and I will try to answer that question. I noted it down to discuss it a little bit if we have the opportunity. I do have serious remarks to state to what you are trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, based on your de facto powers that you were exercising at the time and given at least a mandate that you had from President Karadzic appointing you as the commissioner for Srebrenica, do you think that you might be responsible for the events that occurred in Kravica on the evening or afternoon, late afternoon, that evening in the Kravica warehouse. Yes? No?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. May I augment that briefly? Did I cause this incident in some way? Did I perhaps incite it. Did I try to conceal it? What do you take as my responsibility in that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you can move on. This is involved very complicated legal issues on this matter. So if that is not the gist of your cross-examination, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's -- well, Your Honour. It's a question of command responsibility for the civil authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that, but it's a very complicated question. Let us draw the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could get a couple more facts, Your Honour. I'm not asking for legal conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it not a fact, sir, that with respect to the events that occurred in Kravica, you learned of those events from Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact you discussed those events with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him how it happened, that he should explain it to me. So he explained it to me in the way that he knew how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so you had full knowledge of that as early as the evening of July 13, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More detailed information in the early evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in the Milosevic case, you indicated that based on your conversations that you had with President Karadzic and based on the information that you were getting from Colonel Beara, you came or you made the assumption that Beara was President Karadzic's emissary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in order for us to accept that, we would first have to accept, would we not, that in that conversation, that intercepted conversation, President Karadzic did in fact say to you that someone would be coming with instructions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, if we take out that short sentence and we look at the intercept, as it was recorded by those folks, one could not come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the other hand, if we look at your earlier version where you say again that during that blank space President Karadzic said that he would pass on the instruction to General Mladic with respect to putting those prisoners in the warehouse, one could draw a reasonable conclusion that Beara might have been the emissary of General Mladic, carrying out the order that Karadzic had given Mladic pursuant to your conversation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an assertion, and I don't feel the need to comment on it because I don't think that it's really important. But it's logical to think that that is the right conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to state is that, at least, we have two versions from you. One where Karadzic is saying that he's going to give instructions to Mladic, and then a subsequent one where he says to you, I will send someone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the essence of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And assuming that nothing happened -- there was no conversation other than what we have on the intercept -- in other words, during the three dots where the Prosecution told you that that might have been a space where some lost conversation might have occurred. If we were to accept the paper on its face, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the tenth time this comment has been made. The context has not changed. It's the same thing. It's over and over and over again. I don't mind the point, but let's find a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you may ask a direct question to this witness. There are two kind of statements concerning this incidents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's a third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which is -- or maybe third.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's a third version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which is truthful. This is a very direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is a reason for my questioning. And the third version was where I was trying to make my record, where according to this gentleman's testimony he's been propped by the Prosecution to know that there is a space where potentially conversations might have occurred. And then if we follow on, I have a good-faith basis for laying my foundation. That's all I'm doing, showing the different versions. And I will be quick, five minutes at the most on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to remind you that Mr. Deronjic in this case is not accused, just a witness. And I also have to remind you, there's no need to make some allegations against the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not. Your Honour, he stated that he was told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The question is that we will find the truth in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, did you not earlier testify that when you were going over the intercept with the Prosecution that they alerted you that there could -- that there might have been a gap here, and I'm showing you this gap on the page of this intercept where there are three dots which would convey perhaps some lost conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did talk to the Office of the Prosecutor after I gave my statement, and they thought there was a discrepancy. And we clarified it in the way you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sure you did clarify it with them. But they pointed out to you that in this space which could be a pregnant pause, a long pause, where there's no conversation, they also suggested, did they not, that there could be some lost conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that they suggested I insert this into the text? I already gave an answer, so they couldn't suggest anything of the kind. They maybe suggested one of the possible reasons for gaps in the transcript. I don't really understand what you're asking. It says here: "Drowned out by the teleprinter." That is not audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have to accept -- let's assume that this intercept, as it is, is the true and accurate conversation that you had with President Karadzic. We can then -- can we not then include --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we not then conclude that when Mr. Beara comes to your office and he says to you that he has orders from the top to kill these people, given his position can we not logically conclude that the top would have been Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not conclude that, because although I agree with you it's a logical explanation, but all this is not entirely logical. I remind you again that I gave all my interviews before ever being able to see the transcript. What is interesting is that everything is accurate when compared to the transcript. I stand by what I said at the very outset. Mr. President Karadzic told me, a man would come to see you. That is what I stated and stand by from day one. I never changed anything about that. I described that before I ever got the opportunity to see this. It is a fact that there are gaps and there is a spot when we speak about the prisoners, something is drowned out by the Teletype. Then president continues, a man would come, giving you full instructions, all the goods have to be placed in the storage. Everything seems to fit in logically, despite the gaps. I'm not suggesting anything, but I do assert that I heard that with my own ears. Of course you may have a logic of your own and you can follow it and you can find different explanations. I have nothing against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, let's get one thing clear on the order. On 12 March 2001, before you gave the statements where you claim that those statements are the truth versus the other ones, did you not state that, and I quote, I'm quoting from page 13, line 12, what has been marked as D97, you state: "I accidentally got a text where it was stated that this was recorded, this conversation between me and President Karadzic. I saw that in an office in Belgrade which is devoted to investigation of crimes in Bosnia." So, sir, in fact you had seen that document before you gave your statements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date did you quote? You are walking me from one document to another. Just give me the date of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: March 12th, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer now? Before that I gave how many statements? I cannot really tell you now because I am really tired. How many statements did I give until then? Are you now saying that I never mentioned that conversation until this date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, sir, what I am stating here is that in your previous answer you said that you hadn't had an opportunity to see this intercept before you gave your statements to the Prosecution pursuant to the understanding that you had for your plea agreement. And now I'm showing you -- I'm contradicting you concretely and showing you that you admit to the Prosecutor that you had seen a text of this on 2001. Correct? So you would agree with me that you had seen it. Maybe you forgot, but that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Where did I say that? Where did I say that I had never seen that text before? It's really very difficult for me to follow you across all of these documents. Where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you stated it only two minutes ago, lied on the record here. You stated that you did not see this document, meaning the intercept, before you gave your statements where you claim that President Karadzic told you that somebody would come with instructions. You stated that on the record. That's here today.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How? What do you mean? That's not true. I said that after talking to the Prosecutor - and it is the Office of the Prosecutor who showed me the document - we clarified the issue of these dots, gaps, et cetera. And you see, I said in an earlier interview that I had seen the document. If that was misunderstood, I'm sorry. That's not what I meant to say. I didn't mean to say I had never seen that document before. I only meant that we discussed and clarified the issue of gaps in the conversation during the interviews. If that needs to be corrected, let it be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. And now, if I could go back to your statement in 2002, which would have been after you saw the document, you also injected some language into those gaps. And that's the language that we talked about where you state you conveyed to President Karadzic your concerns, and he says he's going to give instructions to Mladic so that the prisoners could go to the camp or to the prison. That was your understanding. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again I don't have the text in front of me and I have to take your word for it, otherwise I would have to find it. And truth to tell, you don't sometimes quote accurately. You simply give me cause to mistrust you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Deronjic: Earlier in a previous session, did we not discuss this area where I read to you what you stated, that you had concerned with Mr. Mladic, and Karadzic told you that he would send an order? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I don't remember every detail, but I do remember that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And we won't go over it since we covered that area. And I think it's in the record and we can later on find out. Now, in the Milosevic case you were asked a question by the Prosecutor, and I thought -- I would like to get your interpretation. The question was - and I'm reading from the transcript Wednesday, 26 November 2003. It's on page 29.629. And I'll read the question and answer. I'll read it verbatim. It starts on page -- it starts on line 11. "Q. Dealing simply with your last observation about Srebrenica 1995, being a logical finale, the only thing that could result, is that something that you simply judge looking back, or was it something that was in your mind as an observer at the time?" That was the question. And here was your answer according to the transcript. "Your Honour, of course I was a participant in most of these events, and I explained this in my statement in a very precise manner. Of course I thought about everything that was going on during the war as well. But I drew a great many conclusions after all these events when I had the opportunity of having contacts with the Office of the Prosecution that went on from 1997 onwards. I saw a series of documents which explained the situation that I was in from various other aspects. Most of these documents, orders, et cetera, were things I was not aware of at the time when I was engaged in my work that had to do with the war conflict itself." Then there is -- do you remember being asked that question and giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I just want to read the next question to make sure that I'm totally fair with you. The next question is: "I am not sure that that answers the question, but you may say whether you thought about these things at the time and thought that something like this was going to happen or not. But if you don't want to answer further, I won't press you." The Prosecutor didn't want to press you at all in being concrete. Go figure. The answer is: "I have said that I realised many things during the war itself, but that I finally came to my own conclusions after the war operations in the area ended." And then you're thanked by the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice. My question, sir: Would not one get the impression from reading this that as part of your formulation of the conclusions, your opinions, you drew on documents that you either received in the field or looked at in the field, documents you received from the Prosecution, conversations you had with your friendly connections and others, conversations with the Prosecution, where for instance they're pointing out that something might have been left out in the gap, can we not draw that conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which conclusion that is true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That these conclusions are based on a conglomeration of all of this and not based on an independent and reliable memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, it's vague. It's unclear about what conclusion he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm talking about all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At least I'm clear about the scope.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear to me as well, Your Honours, and I will answer the question. It is just by accident that I omitted my own memory when enumerating the sources. Of course I drew on my own memory as well, as well as on subsequent documents, reflections. And in responding to specific questions, I relied on the series of documents that are in the possession of the Prosecution related to this issue. You will notice that in my previous interviews you cannot find this observation because when I was giving my last very voluminous statement of 1999, I didn't have that. But when I saw this series of documents, orders of various units, deployment of various units, et cetera, the conclusion that I cannot help drawing was that it was an extensive, completely misguided campaign that led to the results that we now are familiar with, with the intentions of the author being perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking the question. I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To me, the witness answered the question. There is no need to reconfirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it not logical, sir, for you to fill in the blanks and maybe add to the events as you recall them after seeing documents?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no question of that. I had already by then given my interview without seeing the documents. And I didn't get any other chance. Maybe I would have made certain additions to my interview, but I didn't have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Earlier - and I don't believe it was caught in the translation - but I think you said that you're holding something back in the event -- in the case that you should get indicted for Srebrenica. Did I hear you correctly, that you have -- you're holding back information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did state all the facts and explain them. But there are elements based in law that I could use in my defence case, should the need arise, if I have to defend myself, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we're talking law, not facts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, as I understand it, you were appointed to the presidency of the war council for Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe -- so once you became the president of the war council, your title as commissioner of Srebrenica ceased to exist. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would be fair to conclude, would it not, that you would have known what your mandate was as a commissioner before your subsequent mandate came into play, that is that of the president of the war council?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that from two sources. From my conversation with the president, who clarified certain things for me; and second, I tried to find out what the post of the civilian commissioner implies. And if you want me, I can explain to you in theory what powers I had and what I didn't have. It is a well-known institution that carries with it certain powers. And if you want, I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't need an explanation at this point, but in that appointment there were others appointed as well, were they not, to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you instrumental in selecting those names, or were they loyal SDS party members that Karadzic drew from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best answer I can give you from my recollection is that a lot of problems were involved in the selection. People were angry that I was appointed at all. They were involved in discussions while president talked to me. At one point the president left the office and told us, You have exactly five minutes to reach an agreement and submit a paper. Somehow, at long last, a list of names was drawn up, mainly according to their wishes. I didn't want to get involved very much, and I didn't see any reason to interfere. We tried to get the best possible composition of the war council. I did make several suggestions, and it really was very difficult to make that list, to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the list I note there is one Sretan Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is that the same Sretan Petrovic that you have talked about in one of your statements?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that the same Sretan Petrovic who was wounded during the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you were describing that one of the motivating factors for you to go to Pale on July 7th or 8th or 9th was that their soldiers were getting wounded and, in your opinion, unnecessarily. Was that on the basis of him getting wounded, one of the bases?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the least of my reasons, although it was one of them. But I can't agree that it's the only reason. I explained the reasons already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I guess concretely speaking, was he injured before or after you went to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would ask that we take our break, primarily because -- well, I could go for a little bit longer, but there is some information that is lacking to us. Apparently we have learned that -- from Mr. Deronjic himself that he had an interviewing session on May 4th, 2002. And apparently in the midst of the interview he wished to have the tape recorder shut off. I'm told by the Prosecutor that they have notes that they're trying to gather and have them transcribed for us. I certainly would like to have those notes, because it is subsequent to this period of time when there is a failed negotiation during an untape-recorded session, which Mr. Deronjic has indicated lasted many, many hours. It was subsequent to this that Mr. Deronjic was indicted. So I would like to know what is in the possession of the Prosecution and to see to what extent I should go into it. And there is - now that I think of it - one last matter that we could take at this point. I don't know when we're supposed to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we usually will break in 20 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can use up the last 20 minutes. And then Mr. McCloskey has indicated to me that he has asked that, for that -- those notes to be provided to us, hopefully during the break. And he's rather hopeful, and that's encouraging. And if he's hopeful, I'm hopeful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I turn to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's correct, and I had promised Mr. Karnavas to get those to him shortly after the end of this session so that he would be able to review them for the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas, did you almost cover all the aspects of your cross-examination except one which might need private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for anticipating that, Your Honour. Yes, yes. And I would like to have the caveat since we do have some extra time in the afternoon, during the break, the lunch break, for me to sort of sit down with my co-counsel to figure out if there are any last-minute miscellaneous matters, as I would like to call them, but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I at this moment ask Mr. Stojanovic whether you have any matters that you would like to cross-examine this witness concerning with your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. While preparing for this examination, we agreed to ask only a couple of questions that follow from the last proofing session before the testimony at trial, and that is the conversation that is the interview between Mr. McCloskey and the witness on the 14th of January. That would be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any re-directs, Mr. McCloskey, at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't really see anything at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, there is still 15 minutes left for the morning session. I think we have to make the best use of the time available. Yes, Mr. Karnavas, would you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I suggest that we go into private session as this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. And we'll resume at 3.00 in Courtroom I. The hearing for this morning is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.42 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas. Have you received the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. And I think perhaps it may be more comfortable for Mr. Deronjic, since he doesn't have counsel here, to have this discussion in private session. I leave that up to him. In private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it depends on what kind of question you are going to ask, you know. Because you have to give me somehow a reason so that we could come into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, could we go into private session so I can give you the reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know you're waiting for your own proceedings next week and I know that you're very tired after these four days, but I will try to just put a couple of questions to have you clarify some things for us. The questions relate to the notes from a meeting that you had with Mr. McCloskey on the 14th of January, 2004. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the recent meeting. I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to those notes, it seems that you said that in July 1995, you said that you did not know Dragan Jokic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I just wanted to ask you a couple of questions regarding this. Did you know Dragan Jokic at all during those war years, from 1992 until 1995, or does this only refer to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Jokic until the time he came to the Detention Unit. I didn't know him. I didn't even encounter him. I don't even know if I heard his name, other than in matters relating to the indictment. But I don't remember making a connection between those things. So the answer is negative; I did not know him at all at any time in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned that you saw him for the first time when you, or rather, when he came to the Detention Unit. Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he came I think that that was not the first time, but I think it was after his provisional release, he came to the same floor where I was. That's when we met. We talked during those days, so we got a little bit better acquainted. We have some mutual friends in Zvornik, and this is what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. In view of the fact that we know what your posts were during the war from 1992 until 1995, and in view of the duties that you talked about, did you ever have the opportunity of hearing of any kind of role of Dragan Jokic in the events in Srebrenica in 1992 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never had the opportunity to hear anything about him during the whole war. I did not hear his name, and I did not connect his name in any way to any kind of specific activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are my questions. Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think there is something wrong in the transcript. The question is that: "Did you ever have the opportunity of hearing of any kind of role of Dragan Jokic in the events in Srebrenica in 1995," instead of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. On page 7 [as interpreted], if I am not mistaken, this page of the transcript, it states 1992. I asked from 1992 until the end of 1995. And the answer was, since we're speaking the same language, maybe that's the problem, the answer was: No, I did not. I think that's it, and I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Judges? Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you testified before this Bench that president of the Republika Srpska, one Radovan Karadzic, ordered to kill all Muslim prisoners and refugees in the Srebrenica enclave. In this regard, I would like to know whether you delivered this order to Colonel Blagojevic or discuss this order and details of murder operation when you have met him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I was never -- I never had the opportunity to discuss anything with Mr. Blagojevic. I did not ask for him. I did not look for him. I only saw him on that one occasion that I described. And I did not talk about this with Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And my next question: Do you have specific facts or evidence to indicate that Colonel Blagojevic was directly and actively involved in the crimes which were committed against Muslims from Srebrenica enclave in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, to the extent it was possible, I did do a lot of investigations regarding Srebrenica, and I am stating before this Trial Chamber that I never encountered any fact which would speak to or suggest to me anything of the involvement of Mr. Blagojevic in those crimes. And I would like to add something also. I asked Mr. McCloskey during our last conversation if he could tell me what is Mr. Blagojevic being charged with, what is the basic charge, and what is the possible -- what is the possible evidence against him. And to the extent that he could, he did give me an answer. I am curious, because I really -- I live in Bratunac. I know a lot of people, and I never heard of Mr. Blagojevic, not earlier, nor during that period. I never heard anything that is unpleasant or not nice about Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Hvala hvalum. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. P686, the gazette with the six strategic objectives. 687, Mr. Deronjic's appointment as civil commissioner. 688, the decision on the appointment of Mr. Deronjic to the War Presidency. 689 is the English plea agreement documents. 689/B is the B/C/S version of that. And we have what you had admitted under 92 bis, Ms. Stewart has given 690 as the transcript of Mr. Deronjic's testimony in the Nikolic sentencing. 691 would be the Krstic appeal. 692 is the Milosevic trial. And 693 is the OTP witness statement dated 26 November 2003. All of those last four were the subject of the 92 bis order of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour, to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We believe that those documents are admitted into the evidence. On the part of the Defence, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes there are, Your Honour. Given the extensive line of questioning on the previous statements given by Mr. Deronjic, of course we would be asking that all other statements that we referred to here be also admitted for contextual purposes. I do understand, however, that we have a ruling from prior times that generally, and I underscore generally, those statements are not admissible, but I think this might be one of those occasions where it might be worth having all of them. So I would ask that those be admitted, and I believe it's -- I'm trying to think of whether I have referred to all of these. If I could have a moment. Okay. It would be D92/1, D93/1, D94/1, D95/1, D96/1, D97/1, D98/1, D100/1. I should point out that the D96/1 is the understanding of the parties between the OTP and Mr. Deronjic.
